turns.prompt_text: So if I were to draw 52 cards from a 52 card deck, I imagine there are n factorial possible permutations
turns.response_html:
You are absolutely right. If you are arranging all 52 cards in a specific order, you are looking at 52 factorial ($52!$) possible permutations.

Mathematically, it works because you have 52 choices for the first card, 51 for the second, 50 for the third, and so on:

$$52 \times 51 \times 50 \times \dots \times 1 = 52!$$

The Scale of 52!

To say that $52!$ is a "large number" is perhaps the understatement of the century. It is approximately:

80,658,175,170,943,878,571,660,636,856,403,766,975,289,505,440,883,277,824,000,000,000,000

Or, more simply: $8.06 \times 10^{67}$.

Putting It Into Perspective

To give you an idea of how massive this is, consider this classic thought experiment:

  • The Timer: Set a timer to count down $52!$ seconds.
  • The Walk: Stand on the equator and take one step every billion years.
  • The Ocean: Once you have walked around the entire Earth, take one drop of water out of the Pacific Ocean and keep walking.
  • The Mountain: Once the Pacific Ocean is empty, place a sheet of paper on the ground and refill the ocean.
  • The Result: By the time your stack of paper reaches the Sun, the timer still won't have noticeably changed. You would have to repeat that entire process thousands of times before the countdown hits zero.

Essentially, every time you thoroughly shuffle a deck of cards, it is almost certain that you have created a sequence of cards that has never existed before in the history of the universe and likely never will again.

Are you looking into this for a specific probability problem, or just exploring the mind-boggling world of combinatorics?

turns.prompt_text: Because there are that many possible permutations is something like blackjack or poker not fully predictable by a computer
turns.response_html:
It is a fascinating distinction between computational complexity and predictability. While $52!$ is an astronomical number of possible arrangements, a computer doesn't actually need to "solve" every permutation to master the game.

The predictability of these games depends more on how much information is hidden rather than the total number of ways the deck can be ordered.

Blackjack: Solving the Odds

Blackjack is considered a "solved" or nearly solved game because the dealer’s actions are fixed by strict rules.

  • Combinations vs. Permutations: While there are $52!$ ways to arrange a deck, a computer doesn't care about the order of the 40 cards at the bottom. It only cares about the next card to be dealt.
  • The State Space: Computers use Markov Chains or recursive probability to calculate the "Expected Value" (EV) of every possible hand. Even with a 6-deck shoe, the number of relevant card combinations is large but well within the processing power of a standard laptop.
  • Result: A computer can tell you the mathematically "perfect" move for any given situation (Basic Strategy).

Poker: The Challenge of Incomplete Information

Poker is much harder for computers, but not because of the $52!$ permutations. It is because of Incomplete Information and Game Theory.

  • Hidden Variables: In Poker, you don't know your opponent's cards, and they can lie (bluff).
  • Nash Equilibrium: Instead of predicting the deck, modern AI (like Libratus or Pluribus) uses Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR). It plays against itself trillions of times to find a strategy that is unexploitable, regardless of what the opponent does.
  • Heuristics: Rather than calculating every permutation, the AI groups similar hands together (e.g., a King-high flush and a Queen-high flush are treated similarly) to reduce the "game tree" to a manageable size.

Why the $52!$ Doesn't Protect the Game

In both games, the "search space" is narrowed down significantly:

  1. Relevance: In a hand of Texas Hold'em, only about 7 to 20 cards might ever be seen. We only care about $P(52, 20)$ at most, not the full $52!$.
  2. Frequency: The computer doesn't need to know the exact sequence; it only needs to know the probability distribution of the remaining cards.

So, while a computer can't tell you exactly which card is next in a truly randomized deck (that's physics/shuffling, not math), it can play so close to "perfectly" that it will statistically win over any human in the long run.

Does the idea of a "perfect" strategy make the game less interesting to you, or is the math behind the "unexploitable" play what draws you in?

turns.prompt_text: Is it possible for a human to be able to play a perfect game of blackjack?
turns.response_html:
It is entirely possible for a human to play what is mathematically defined as a "perfect" game of blackjack, but it requires distinguishing between Basic Strategy and Advantage Play.

1. Basic Strategy: The "Human Perfect"

A human can achieve 100% accuracy in "Basic Strategy." This is a mathematically derived set of rules that tells you the optimal move (Hit, Stand, Double Down, or Split) for every possible combination of your hand versus the dealer's upcard.

  • Memorization: The strategy is typically condensed into a grid. Because the dealer's actions are automated, the math for every scenario is fixed. A human can memorize this chart perfectly with enough practice.
  • The Result: By playing Basic Strategy, a human reduces the house edge to its absolute minimum—usually around 0.5% (depending on the specific table rules).

2. Card Counting: The "Optimal Perfect"

To actually have an edge over the casino, a human must track the ratio of high cards to low cards remaining in the deck. This is "perfect" play in the sense that you are no longer just reacting to the cards on the table, but predicting the likelihood of future cards.

  • Complexity: Unlike a computer, a human cannot remember every single card dealt in a six-deck shoe. Instead, they use "heuristics" like the Hi-Lo System, where cards 2–6 are (+1), 10–A are (-1), and 7–9 are (0).
  • Execution: A human can execute this perfectly, but it requires intense mental fatigue and "emotional" perfection—ignoring the stress of losing hands while knowing the math is in your favor long-term.

The Catch: Perfection $\neq$ Certainty

In the world of probability, "perfect play" does not mean "winning every hand." Even if you play with a computer’s precision:

  • Variance: You can play a hand perfectly and still lose because the next card is random.
  • The House Edge: Even with perfect Basic Strategy, the house still has a fractional advantage. You aren't "beating" the game; you are just losing as slowly as possible.
  • Casino Interference: Casinos look for "perfect" players. If a human plays with robotic accuracy and varies their bets based on the count, they are often identified by surveillance and asked to leave.

Summary

Strategy LevelHumanly Possible?Outcome
Basic StrategyYes (Easy)Minimizes house edge to ~0.5%.
Card CountingYes (Hard)Flips the edge to ~1–2% in favor of the human.
Shuffle TrackingRarely (Expert)Extremely difficult; tracking physical clusters of cards.

So, while a human can match a computer's decision-making in blackjack, they can never match a computer's stamina. A human will eventually make a "fatigue error," whereas a computer will play its billionth hand with the same precision as its first.

turns.prompt_text: What is Shuffle tracking also with card counting, would that require the player sing every single card that is dealt.
turns.response_html:
Both Card Counting and Shuffle Tracking are "Advantage Play" techniques, but they rely on different principles. While they both require you to pay close attention to the cards, they don't necessarily require you to "memorize" every card in the way a computer would. Instead, they rely on data compression and observation.

1. Card Counting: The Statistical Approach

Card counting doesn't involve memorizing that the "Jack of Hearts" was dealt. Instead, you use a heuristic (a mental shortcut) to track the ratio of high cards (10s and Aces) to low cards (2s through 6s).

  • The Goal: High cards favor the player (better chance for Blackjacks and dealer busts). Low cards favor the dealer.
  • The Method: Most counters use the Hi-Lo System. Every card is assigned a value of $+1$, $0$, or $-1$.
    • Low Cards (2–6): $+1$ (The deck is getting better for you as these leave).
    • Neutral Cards (7–9): $0$
    • High Cards (10–A): $-1$ (The deck is getting worse as these leave).
  • Do you need to see every card? Yes. To maintain an accurate "Running Count," you must see every card that comes out of the shoe. If you miss a few cards, your statistical edge disappears because your "data set" is incomplete.

2. Shuffle Tracking: The Physical Approach

Shuffle tracking is significantly more difficult than card counting. It assumes that shuffles are not perfectly random. If a dealer shuffles "lazily," clusters of cards (called slugs) might stay together.

  • The Goal: Identify a cluster of high cards (a "rich slug") as they are put into the discard tray, and then track where that physical "clump" ends up after the shuffle.
  • The Method:
    1. Observation: You watch the discard tray and notice that the last few hands had a lot of 10s and Aces.
    2. Visual Tracking: You watch the dealer's hands during the shuffle. You track that specific "rich" section of the deck as it is split, riffled, and restacked.
    3. The Cut: If you can track where the rich slug landed, you try to "cut" the deck so that the high-card cluster is at the top of the shoe, ready to be dealt first.
  • Do you need to see every card? Not exactly. You only need to see the cards clearly enough to identify where the high-density clusters are. You aren't tracking individual values as much as you are tracking "zones" of the deck.

Comparison: Do you have to "See Everything"?

TechniqueRequires Seeing Every Card?Mental EffortPrimary Skill
Card CountingYes. You need the sum of every card dealt to know the current probability.Moderate (Arithmetic)Basic Math & Concentration
Shuffle TrackingYes/Partial. You need to see the discards to identify slugs and then watch the shuffle.Extreme (Visual/Spatial)Visual Mapping & Kinetic Tracking

The "Mental Load" Myth

People often assume card counters are like Rain Man, memorizing the sequence of 312 cards (6 decks). In reality, a counter is just doing simple addition and subtraction.

If you are a counter, you don't see:

"King of Clubs, 2 of Hearts, 5 of Diamonds, Ace of Spades..."

You see:

"$-1, +1, +1, -1...$ The count is still zero."

It’s much more like a running tally than a photographic memory. Does the idea of tracking "zones" of a deck for shuffle tracking sound more like a visual puzzle or a physics problem to you?
